title: Markets and Fairs
objective: After this level you can describe medieval markets and trade fairs.
summary: English markets met weekly by royal charter; fairs met yearly on saints’ days. The Champagne fairs linked north and south, and piepowder courts gave quick justice.

cards.headline: Medieval England had courts named after dusty feet.
cards.body: They sat right at the fairs, settling traders’ arguments on the spot. To see why anyone needed them, follow the money: first to the weekly market, then to the great fairs.

cards.headline: Market day
cards.body: A medieval market wasn’t open every day. In England it met once a week, on a set day and in a set place, and holding one took a royal charter. Towns, villages and monasteries all won them. From 1200 there was a catch: a new market was allowed only if it didn’t harm the markets nearby. Even medieval kings worried about the shop down the road.

cards.headline: Fair season
cards.body: A fair was bigger and rarer: once a year, usually on a saint’s feast day, lasting from a single day to a week or more. The greatest were the Champagne fairs in France, which rotated among four towns, Lagny, Bar-sur-Aube, Provins and Troyes, and peaked in the 13th century. Under the count’s protection, merchants swapped northern cloth for spices and dyes from the Mediterranean. North met south in a French field.

cards.headline: Credit and quick justice
cards.body: Big deals needed trust. At the Champagne fairs, bargains often ran on letters of credit rather than bags of coins, laying groundwork for modern credit. And when a deal went wrong in England, a piepowder court (from the French for “dusty feet”) settled disputes at fairs and markets fast and on the spot, before the traveller could dust off and leave.
cards.callout: A weekly market for the neighbourhood; a yearly fair for the wider world

cards.headline: Markets and fairs: understood
learned: English markets met weekly, by royal charter
Fairs met yearly, usually on a saint’s day
The Champagne fairs linked northern cloth and Mediterranean spices
Piepowder courts gave quick justice at fairs

questions.prompt: How often did a typical medieval English market meet?

options.label: Every day except Sunday
options.rationale: Markets kept a single set day.

options.label: Once a week, on a set day
Once a year, on a saint’s day
Only when the king visited
options.rationale: Markets ran on a fixed schedule.

questions.explanation: An English market met once a week, on a set day and in a set place.

questions.prompt: What made the Champagne fairs so important to medieval trade?

options.label: They were the only place anyone could buy bread
options.rationale: Bread was bought at local markets.

options.label: They were held every week in Paris
options.rationale: They rotated among four other towns.

options.label: Kings used them to collect taxes on wool
options.rationale: They were about trade between merchants.

options.label: Northern cloth met Mediterranean spices and dyes there

questions.explanation: Under the count’s protection, merchants from north and south traded cloth for spices and dyes, often on credit.

questions.prompt: Level 51’s towns won their freedoms in charters. How did an English town or village win the right to hold a weekly market?

options.label: A vote of everyone in the county
A letter of credit from a merchant
options.rationale: Credit paid for deals, not markets.

options.label: A ruling from a piepowder court
options.rationale: Those courts settled disputes at markets.

questions.explanation: Like the communes of Level 51, an English market rested on a charter: a royal grant of the right to hold it.
